entries.title: Paste cited code into a review rounds context
entries.brief: Reviewers edit nothing and review a fixed commit, so code pasted at round start cannot go stale; measure it against todays reviewer
entries.body:
## Seen

Note `kickstart-per-card` rejects pasting span code into a Webster fork's pack: the code goes stale as earlier cards edit the files, and Claude Code refuses an Edit on a file the agent has not read itself, so an implementer must read every file it edits anyway.
Neither reason holds for a reviewer: it edits nothing, and it reviews a fixed commit, so code pasted at the round's start cannot drift during the round.

## Operator view, not a decision (2026-10-15)

For reviewers it may be different: they could get the code the target cites pasted in, instead of reading it themselves.

## Operator decision this note must answer (2026-10-16)

From the stencil intent audit of 2026-10-15 (now in note `webster-fork-stencil-fixes`): code text is never pasted into a prompt without a good reason, and the reason is written down.
Before this note is built, it states its good reason for pasting code into a review round against that decision.

## Earlier data

Note `fan-master-preread` records one hand-built try on solo `opus[medium]` Discussion review (2026-10-10, one run on the `webster-replan-state` fixture): a body dump of the 35 cited symbols, about 20k tokens in a file read first, cost about the same as a kick-start pack of spans and missed the BLOCKING finding the span pack found.
One run per arm is too few to decide anything.

## Idea

Give a review round, Webster-Review or Merge-Review first, since their target is a diff at a fixed commit, the bodies of the symbols the target changes or cites, rendered by lyx at round start, and measure finding quality and cost against today's reviewer.

## Problem raised by the operator (2026-10-15)

A reviewer often finds it must explore more code than it was given.
Code pasted into its context does not count as read the way its own Read calls do, so it cannot tell what it already holds: it may re-read pasted code or miss that a span is already there.

Possible answer (the orch's idea, not discussed): label each pasted block with its file and line range, and open the paste with a list of every file and range it holds, so the reviewer checks that list before a read.
The `fan-master-preread` lab used the same kind of reading manifest for forks; whether reviewers follow it is untested.

## A glyph pack for reviewers (from note `glyph-use-audit`, 2026-10-15)

The Burler side of the kick-start pack, issue #228: a pack of the reviewed glyphs injected once before the reviewer's explore phase, so every lens fork inherits it (the operator's architecture correction on #228).
Measured basis from before: quarry's `results/2026-09-06-kickstart` (`bench/loomyard-eval/ladder/results/2026-09-06-kickstart/conclusion.md`, commit `d2e492d`).
The Webster pack audits (`docs/research/glyph-audit-2026-10-12`, `-10-13`, `-10-15`) found too little gain to build it yet: forks read about 20 % less but explore as much.
Take it up only if the per-card pack of task `kickstart-per-card` shows a clear gain when measured with `tools/forkaudit`.

### The pack is the read set (was note pack-is-the-read-set)

Seen in fan-lab 2026-10-10: a solo `opus[medium]` reviewer given a kick-start pack ("read all listed spans first") read the pack and then explored about 20 more tool calls, so the pack came on top of exploration instead of replacing it.
Neither the prompt nor the ladder card said to stay with the pack.

The reviewer prompt would say the pack is the read set:
- the reviewer reads the pack's spans and treats them as read;
- any read beyond them needs a named gap (a caller or spawned process one hop out), within a small tool-call budget;
- the reviewer ends with one line per extra read saying why the pack lacked it (the fork rule from `fan-master-preread` variant D).

entries.title: creel stage 2: orch and batten notices through creel
entries.brief: The orch watcher and batten notices and injects go through creel; the watcher keeps only its cycle logic
entries.body:
## Goal

Creel stage 2: system notices go through creel.
The design is in `creel-core`'s body until that task lands, then in the creel package's `doc.go`.

## Operator decision (2026-10-15)

Creel is a prerequisite for Codex and is built in its three stages (operator, 2026-10-06).

## Scope (stage 2 of the creel design)

The orch watcher's and batten's notices and the watcher's injects go through creel, and the watcher's notice queue and idle probe go.
The watcher keeps only its cycle logic (tracking tokens, choosing `refresh`/`distill`/automatic cycles, waiting for the note, sequencing the reload, its state and lifecycle), and advances a cycle phase only on the orch's reply to the note request, or once creel confirms a command inject was typed.
The note request is mail, answered by post (`written <path>` or `defer`).

## Operator decision (2026-10-15): a note until creel has proven itself

This stage replaces paths that work today, so it stays a note, which never starts, until `creel-core` has landed and creel has proven itself; the operator then promotes it.
When promoted, it depends on `creel-core`.

## Operator decision (2026-10-17): nothing durable lives only in creel

This task extends `PATTERN-durable-vs-ephemeral-state` in the same commit as its code, with this text:
"Nothing a run, the orch or a landing depends on lives only under `.lyx`: decisions, landings, stop reports and board state are always in git (board, records, decision record), and never-tracked state such as the creel journal and the notice log is a delivery path or cache that a fresh machine starts without."
Background (orch, 2026-10-17): the creel journal sits in `<hub>/_board/.lyx/creel/journal/`, never tracked, so a move to another machine leaves undelivered mail behind; the strands it was meant for do not move either, and the orch reads landings from the board.

## Orch recommendation, not a decision (2026-10-17): the notice log goes

Once batten's notices are creel mail to the orch, a notice stays unread until the orch reads it, so batten's copy in the prime's `.lyx/notices.log` (`shedrun.NoticeLog`) is redundant.
The task removes it, and the orch role's fallback reads unread creel mail instead.

## Promoted (operator, 2026-10-17)

Creel proved itself: the C13 re-test (`docs/research/creel-audit-2026-10-17/`), the creel CLI fixes, and the llm smoke `TestSmokeCreelClaudeStrand` green on the operator's run.
The operator promoted this stage on 2026-10-17, with the reminder change below folded in.

## Reminders carry no content (folded in from note `creel-reminder-no-subject`)

### Seen (orch, 2026-10-17)

A demo post from `ly:orch` to a fresh Claude strand `ly:demo` was reminded as:
`[creel] 1 unread: #3 from ly:orch «Hello from ly:orch via creel. Please reply to this message with: lyx creel post » — run lyx creel read`.
This is the documented design (`internal/creelengine/doc.go`, the reminder paragraph): the subject is the body's first line, cut at 80 runes, inside « ».
A message without a separate first line therefore shows its content in the reminder, and the receiving agent can act on it without running `lyx creel read`.

### Operator decision (2026-10-17)

Creel's reminder carries no message content, only the count, ids and senders; urgent content goes by inject.

### Operator view, not a decision (2026-10-17)

The receiver has to ask for the content actively with `lyx creel read`.
A reminder can reach an agent in the middle of a run, busy with something else: it should only learn that one or more messages wait, and choose itself when it has the time and capacity to read them.
Part of a message arriving with the reminder is clutter and confuses the agent.
Something the agent must read at once goes by `lyx creel inject` instead (with `--interrupt` when the running turn must stop first).

### Idea

- The reminder names only the count, ids and senders, such as `[creel] 1 unread: #3 from ly:orch — run lyx creel read`.
- `lyx creel log` keeps its subjects, since only the operator and the orch read the journal.

### Open

- The reminder is typed only at idle, but in Claude a typed line starts a new turn, so even a content-free reminder takes the agent's next turn: whether stencils should tell agents that a reminder may be left until their current task is done.
- Whether the journal's `subject` field stays as the body's first line or goes too.

entries.title: creel stage 3: agents message through creel, not SendMessage
entries.brief: Parent asks, parent review, stop reports and shuttle send go through creel, so a non-Claude engine can take a role with a parent
entries.body:
## Goal

Creel stage 3: agents reach their parent and each other through creel, not Claude Code's `SendMessage`, so a non-Claude engine can take a role that has a parent.
The design is in `creel-core`'s body until that task lands, then in the creel package's `doc.go`.

## Operator decision (2026-10-15)

Creel is a prerequisite for Codex; the Codex-readiness plan's interim `neutral-parent-asks` is dropped in favour of this stage.

## Scope (stage 3 of the creel design, plus the Codex-readiness findings)

- The parent-review gate (`internal/parentreview/gate.go`, which today prompts Discussion-Write to `SendMessage` the parent) posts itself.
- Drivers' stop reports post instead of duplicating batten's notices over `SendMessage`.
- `lyx shuttle send` and `lyx shuttle interrupt` move behind creel.
- The parent directive (`contracts/stencils/parent/parent-directive-parent.md`), rendered for every role with a parent, says to ask through creel, not "by `SendMessage`".
- `shuttleengine/hold.go`'s hold notice names creel, not `SendMessage`.
- The other stencils that name `SendMessage` (`seat-directive-{chair,advisor}`, `shed-template-driver-notify{,-watched}.md`, `loom-template-parent-review-delivery.md`, the orch role) move to creel where the Discussion finds it fits; what stays Claude-only is declared through `Spec.Requires`.

## Risk to check in Discussion

The hold notice goes to the prime orch (`orchcli.NotifyPrime`), while the parent directive names `parent_name`, which may be a loom driver strand: check per recipe that a question reaches the session that answers it.

## Operator decision (2026-10-15): a note until creel has proven itself

This stage replaces paths that work today, so it stays a note, which never starts, until creel has proven itself; the operator then promotes it.
When promoted, it depends on `creel-notices` and `engine-config-seams`.

## Reply discipline (folded in from note `creel-reply-discipline`, operator decision 2026-10-17)

The operator decided on 2026-10-17 that this belongs in stage 3.

### Seen (orch, 2026-10-17)

In a demo, `ly:orch` posted #3 to a fresh Claude strand `ly:demo`, whose body asked for a reply by `lyx creel post --reply`; the agent read it and replied as #4.
It replied by post only because the body told it how.
An inject (#5) asking for `PONG` was answered in the receiver's own pane, to the operator, and never reached the sender: an inject is typed as a user line and has no reply path.
`lyx creel read` prints the message with its id but says nothing about answering by `post --reply`.
Creel already limits inject: only EXTERNAL callers, programs and orch strands may inject into another strand (`lyx creel inject --help`).

### Operator view, not a decision (2026-10-17)

Creel needs a strict regime, so that an agent that sends something to another agent never ends up without an answer because the receiver wrote its answer in its own pane, to the operator.
Inject and post are two different things.
An inject looks as if the operator typed it, and that is its point.
A post takes an active step by the receiver to fetch it, and that step should tell the agent the message came from outside, not from the operator, so it cannot answer by writing in its pane.

### Orch view on that

The split holds, but the agent should be told rather than left to infer it: the reminder that starts its turn is itself typed into the pane like an operator line, and a model answers in its pane by default.
One line in `lyx creel read`'s output (the sender is another strand, not the operator; answer with `lyx creel post --reply <id> <text>`) makes it explicit at the moment it matters.

### Idea (orch recommendation)

- `lyx creel read` prints, with each message, the command that answers it (`lyx creel post --reply <id> <text>`), and says when the sender waits on the reply (`--wait-reply`).
- The agent stencils state the rule once, in a shared block: a creel message is answered by `post --reply`, never in the pane; a line in the pane is for the operator.
- An inject never carries a question that expects an answer from the receiver; a sender that wants an answer posts.
- A message whose sender waits and that goes unanswered past a bound is journaled, so the orch can see it.

### Operator idea (2026-10-17): reply expected, chased

- `post` takes a flag marking that the sender expects a reply, without blocking the sender the way `--wait-reply` does.
- Creel already journals `read` and links a reply to its message by `reply_to`, so it knows when an expected reply is owed.
- When no reply is sent within a set time after the receiver read the message, creel types a reminder of its own, such as `Sender expected a reply to #<id> from <sender>`.

Orch recommendation on the idea:
- `--wait-reply` implies the flag, so a waiting sender gets the chase too.
- The chase follows the reminder rules: typed only at idle, no message content, and `read` shows the expected-reply mark and the reply command.
- Chases are bounded (one or two), after which creel journals the message as unanswered and tells the sender, so a dead receiver never makes a chase loop.
- The time limit is a creel config key.

Operator view, not a decision (2026-10-17): all of this must be logged, including how often creel has to chase.

Orch recommendation on the logging:
- The journal gets an event per chase (`chased`, with the message id, receiver and chase number) and one `unanswered` event when the chases run out; `lyx creel log --id <id>` then shows a message's whole path, posted, read, chased, replied or unanswered.
- A report, beside `lyx report convergence`, counts expected replies, chases and unanswered messages per receiver role, so the stencils of roles that often need chasing can be tuned.

### Open

- The flag's name, and whether a reply by `defer` (as in the orch's note request) counts as an answer.

entries.title: Module labels from what a task touches, not only what it is about
entries.brief: Half the landings that changed the shuttle core lacked the shuttle label; derive or check module labels from the plan and the diff
entries.body:
## Seen (count, 2026-10-15)

Of 50 landings on `main` from 2026-10-05 to 2026-10-15 that changed non-test Go code in `internal/shuttleengine/*.go`, 47 were matched to their task through the closing PR comment, and only 24 of those carried the `shuttle` label.
The others carried labels for what the task was about (`reed`, `loom`, `burler`, `batten`, `stencil`), not for every package its diff touched: `run-pane-timing`, `overview-seats`, `hibernate-trigger`, `merge-review`, `twill-discusser` and `small-fixes-batch` among them.
The board's module labels are set by hand when an entry is written, before anyone knows which packages the work will touch.
The orch bundles tasks and sets `depends_on` by package overlap read from labels, so a label that misses a touched module hides an overlap.
Counted by Haiku agents from the board history and `gh pr list`; scripts and tables in `.scratch/label-count/` in the prime, not committed.

## Idea

- Derive a task's module labels, or check them, from what the work touches: the plan's `Edit:`/`Create:` paths once Plan-Write has run, and the landed diff at landing.
- At least, record the touched modules on the landed entry or in the run record, so overlap checks and reports read facts, not the labels written up front.
- Whether a mismatch only warns, adds the label, or feeds the orch's overlap check is open.

entries.title: Start one task per overlapping group at a newly-ready start
entries.brief: When a landing makes several overlapping tasks ready at once, batten starts one per group and names the rest in its notice
entries.body:
Split from `sibling-overlap-check` on 2026-10-15; the operator decided only the board warning and skill rule there.

## Idea

When a landing makes several tasks ready at once, batten starts one task per group of overlapping tasks (shared module labels, later the paths of note `labels-from-diff`) and leaves the rest for the orch, naming the overlap in the notice.

entries.title: Classify Plan lens and review findings to make the Plan writer get it right first
entries.brief: Find what Plan lenses and Plan-Burler-Review keep catching, and stop each recurring class at the writer
entries.body:
## Seen (2026-10-15)

Over the 15 most recent full loom runs (`tools/tokencount/tokencount.sh -last 15`), Plan cost about $13 a run: the plan lead about $5.50, its forks (fork0 and the five lens forks) about $4, and Plan-Burler-Review about $3.80.
Each fix the lenses or the review ask for is work the writer did not get right the first time.

## Operator view, not a decision (2026-10-15)

Plan is heavy by nature, since it turns the Discussion into concrete work; the aim is a smarter Plan writer, so fewer Burler rounds are needed.

## Idea (orch recommendation)

- A fresh agent classifies every finding the Plan lenses and Plan-Burler-Review raised in recent runs: what kind of defect, whether it was real, and whether the review found something the lenses had not.
- Each recurring class goes where it is cheapest to stop at the source:
  - a machine check in `lyx loom validate-plan`, when the class can be checked deterministically;
  - a writer rule in the Plan stencil, when it is a judgement the writer can make up front;
  - a missing input, when the writer lacked something it needed (for example what `discussion-relevant-list` now hands it).
- Then measure whether lens and review findings per run drop.

## Operator view, not a decision (2026-10-16)

The lens fan and twill fixer (`fan-prompt-tuning`) are built first.
Later, this audit runs over real runs made with them, and the wording of the reviewer and fixer prompts is adjusted from what it observes, beside the Plan writer measures above.

## Operator decision (2026-10-16)

The Discussion and Plan perches run the twill fixer in every round; the lens fan reviewer runs in round 1 only, with solo review from round 2.
Reason: fixers introduce many defects, and a defect a late-round fixer introduces is seen only by the next review, or not at all at the hard cap.
The hub's `loom.yaml` carries it as `discussion_fan: ["review-discussion", ""]`, `plan_fan: ["review-plan", ""]`, `discussion_fix_fan: fix-discussion` and `plan_fix_fan: fix-plan`.
Orch recommendation, not a decision: the audit compares late-round fixer defects against runs from before this setup.

# Moved from note `perch-review-analysis` (issue #676, 2026-10-16)

The analysis measured rounds, tokens and late BLOCKING findings per perch; its classification of the late BLOCKING findings moved to `fan-prompt-tuning`, the lens fan and twill fixer it proposed are built there, and its proposal of two parallel round-1 reviewers is replaced by the lens fan.
Its Webster proposal (a hard cap of 2) is already met by the hub's `loom.yaml`: `webster_max_bounces: 1` with `webster_auto_accept: true`.
Two of its proposals are left for this audit to weigh, numbered as in the original:

3. **Later rounds review the fix delta.**
   A findings cannot be caught in round 1; they need a round after the fix.
   From round 2, one reviewer checks only what the fixer changed plus the sibling decisions or cards it touches, which is cheaper than a full review.
   Compare Traycer's incremental re-verify in #671.
6. **Measure again in a week**, with the same scripts: rounds per perch, BLOCKING share in round 1, and tokens per perch, before and after twill and the changes above.

entries.title: Ideas to borrow from comparable agent orchestrators (survey, Oct 2026)
entries.body:
Imported from [issue #671](https://github.com/Knatte18/loomyard/issues/671).

This issue collects features from comparable open-source agent orchestrators that LoomYard could borrow later.
I surveyed each project's README, docs and some source through the GitHub API, plus a few vendor docs pages and fresh web searches, in October 2026.
I left out anything LoomYard already has: a deterministic phase engine, glyph-validated plans, independent review with a judge and a bounce budget, warp/weft records in git, per-task worktree pairs, creel, tender, the self-cycling orch, and severity-tagged review findings with BLOCKING verdicts.
Where LoomYard already solves the same problem another way, the bullet says so, since the other project's approach may still hold something to improve.
Each bullet names its source and the LoomYard module it would touch.
Nothing here is a commitment; these are leads to triage.

## Plan validation and concurrency (quarry, Plan-Write, Batchifier, board)

- **Typed scope operations on cards** — [foremerge](https://github.com/naw103/foremerge) (`docs/conflict-detection.md`, `src/conflict.rs`).
  Each declared scope carries an operation: additive (`add`, `extend`, `modify`) or breaking (`replace`, `remove`, `rename`, `migrate`).
  Deterministic rules flag destructive-vs-additive and divergent-rewrite collisions, even when the files do not overlap.
  LoomYard already types its cards (Create/Edit/Delete/Rename/Move), keeps overlapping tasks apart through board labels, and runs the alignment gate before plan writing and before merge.
  Worth comparing: whether foremerge's operation-pair rules catch a collision the board labels and the alignment gate would miss.
- **Symbol leases between concurrent tasks** — [Fusion](https://github.com/Runfusion/Fusion) (`packages/core/src/tasks/symbol-lock-types.ts`, `file-scope-lease.ts`).
  Durable, expiring leases on symbol keys serialize tasks whose claims overlap.
  Ties are broken deterministically by priority, then age, then id.
  LoomYard covers the same need with board labels that keep overlapping tasks from running in parallel, plus the merge conflict resolver.
  Worth comparing: symbol-level granularity versus label-level, and the deterministic tie-break.
  [ORCH](https://github.com/oxgeneral/ORCH) (`src/domain/scope.ts`) does a cruder glob-prefix version.
- **Requirement-to-card traceability gate** — [Spec Kit](https://github.com/github/spec-kit) `/analyze` (`templates/commands/analyze.md`) and [Kiro](https://kiro.dev/docs/specs/correctness/).
  Spec Kit reports requirement→task coverage % and terminology drift; Kiro links each property test to a requirement and a task.
  For LoomYard: give decision-record decisions IDs and have the Plan-Write gate refuse a plan with an uncovered decision or a card that traces to none.
- **Criterion amendment ledger** — [oh-my-claudecode](https://github.com/Yeachan-Heo/oh-my-claudecode) (`skills/ralph/SKILL.md`, `docs/adr/03664-ralph-prd-criterion-amendment.md`).
  An acceptance criterion can only be relaxed through a recorded amendment that keeps the original text, reason, evidence and authority.
  For LoomYard: webster and the Webster-review judge could refuse a card whose acceptance text changed without such an entry in weft.
- **Blast-radius verdict per glyph** — [tree-sitter-analyzer](https://github.com/aimasteracc/tree-sitter-analyzer).
  Impact analysis returns SAFE/CAUTION/UNSAFE for an edit target.
  For LoomYard: a `quarry impact <glyph>` that Plan review reads, beyond the existing existence check.
- **Bugfix spec with fail-on-base test** — [Kiro bugfix specs](https://kiro.dev/docs/specs/bugfix-specs/).
  Current / Expected / Unchanged behaviour in WHEN/THEN form, each becoming a test.
  For LoomYard: a bugfix stencil for Discussion-Write, plus a Go gate that the new test fails on the base commit and passes on the tip.

## Review gates (burler, Bouncer, gate)

- **Cross-model external review with rebuttal** — [ralphex](https://github.com/umputun/ralphex) (README "Custom External Review", `pkg/config/defaults/prompts/codex.txt`).
  Any script that prints `file:line - issue` or `NO ISSUES FOUND` can review the diff.
  Claude fixes each finding or argues against it, and the rebuttal goes into the next round.
  Round 1 reviews the full branch diff; later rounds review only the fixes.
  For LoomYard: a non-Claude reviewer as a second shuttle engine inside a review segment, for independence across model families.
- **Stalemate detection** — ralphex `--review-patience=N`.
  It stops after N rounds that produce no commit and no tree change.
  For LoomYard: the Bouncer could halt a segment before it exhausts its bounce budget.
- **Review verdict bound to content** — [Fusion](https://github.com/Runfusion/Fusion) (`docs/workflow-steps.md` "Content-binding review proof", `packages/core/src/planner/plan-approval.ts`).
  An approval records a fingerprint of the plan or diff, and merge refuses a stale or unprovable approval.
  For LoomYard: stamp each Bouncer verdict in weft with the warp tree SHA and have Publish/PR-Gate refuse one that no longer matches.
  Check first whether webster's plan fingerprint already covers the plan side.
- **Incremental re-verify and "Outdated" findings** — [Traycer](https://docs.traycer.ai/extension/tasks/verification.md) and Fusion's severity-gated verdicts.
  A re-review checks only earlier findings and marks them resolved or outdated; Fusion forbids new non-blocking findings on a re-review.
  For LoomYard: a cheaper re-review round mode for burler, to cut circling.
- **Quorum of differently-angled judges** — [ccswarm](https://github.com/nwiizo/ccswarm) Sangha (`crates/ccswarm/src/workflow/sangha.rs`).
  N read-only members (planner, reviewer, QA) each emit `APPROVE|REVISE`, and the stage passes on quorum.
  For LoomYard: an optional multi-judge Bouncer for high-risk segments.
  ccswarm itself has not implemented dissent resolution yet.
- **Post-implementation convergence check** — [Spec Kit](https://github.com/github/spec-kit) `/converge` (`templates/commands/converge.md`).
  It classifies gaps as missing, partial, contradicts or **unrequested**, ignores checkbox claims as evidence, and appends a remediation phase rather than free-form fixes.
  For LoomYard: an "unrequested" lens in Webster review against the decision record, to catch scope creep.
- **Risk tier by changed paths** — [yylo](https://github.com/yylo-dev/yylo) (`src/templates/config/risk-policy.json`).
  Globs over auth, migrations, lockfiles and CI pick the reviewer count and whether the full suite runs.
  For LoomYard: choose a segment's review depth and `lyx gate test` scope from the diff.
  yylo has since marked this queue as retired (`docs/lifecycle-simplification-migration.md`), so treat it as an idea only.
- **Pre-existing failure baseline** — oh-my-claudecode `ralph verify --write-baseline`.
  Gates fail only on new failures; baseline failures become warnings.
  For LoomYard: `lyx gate test` and the webster verify gate could record a base-commit baseline, so implementers stop chasing failures that were already red.
  Counterpoint: LoomYard holds that main is always green, so a baseline would legitimize a red main, and it costs an extra full suite run before work starts.
- **Typed completion signals** — [Bernstein](https://github.com/sipyourdrink-ltd/bernstein) janitor (`src/bernstein/core/quality/janitor.py`).
  A task declares `path_exists`, `test_passes` or `file_contains`; an LLM judge runs only once those pass.
  For LoomYard: cards could declare done-conditions that `record-batch` checks in Go.

## Engine, recipes and governance (shed, tender, orch, board)

- **Hard token and cost budgets** — Fusion per-task budgets (`docs/settings-reference.md#per-task-token-budget`) and [Conductor](https://github.com/microsoft/conductor) `limits.budget_usd` with `budget_mode: audit|enforce` (`docs/workflow-syntax.md`).
  A soft cap alerts once, and a hard cap pauses with a named reason.
  Conductor recommends running in audit mode first.
  For LoomYard: weft already records token usage per round; shed or tender could enforce a per-run cap, starting in audit mode.
- **Cross-run quarantine** — Bernstein (`src/bernstein/core/security/quarantine.py`).
  A task that fails 3 times across runs is skipped or decomposed, and the entry expires after 7 days; host-resource failures are excused.
  For LoomYard: board plus orch, so the orch stops relaunching a doomed task.
- **Abandon as a terminal state with a closed reason list** — Bernstein (`docs/operations/abandonments.md`).
  `ABANDONED` is distinct from `FAILED`, and dependent tasks cascade to `BLOCKED_BY_ABANDON`.
  For LoomYard: shed's terminal outcomes, board dependencies and `report convergence`.
- **Fork a run from a step with a tree snapshot** — Bernstein (`docs/operations/fork-from-step.md`).
  The worktree is snapshotted to `refs/bernstein/snapshots/<run>/<step>` at each step.
  For LoomYard: `shed goto` moves the cursor but does not restore the warp tree; a per-producer ref would.
- **Warm retry guarded by a workspace hash** — Bernstein (`docs/operations/checkpointed-retries.md`).
  A retry resumes or forks the native session only if the workspace hash has not changed, and otherwise falls back to a cold restart.
  For LoomYard: webster's fork recovery.
- **Per-run pinning of prompts** — Conductor `bundle build`; Bernstein refuses to resume after its spec digest changes.
  For LoomYard: record the stencil digests a run started with in weft and have resume warn on drift, complementing `lyx stencil diff`.
- **Evidence reuse by input identity** — yylo (`risk_policy.py` `semantic_reuse_decision`).
  Earlier test or review evidence is reused only if its inputs and prompt identity are unchanged; a changed review prompt reruns only the review.
  For LoomYard: shed resume and the gate after a rework.
- **Recipe validator and non-LLM step types** — Conductor `conductor validate` and its script/set steps.
  It catches unreachable steps, bad route targets and undeclared inputs offline, and script steps route on exit code or stdout JSON.
  For LoomYard: extend the shed recipe validator with reachability and stencil output-name checks; a generic script producer could route on `lyx gate test`.
- **Mid-run guidance at the next step boundary** — Conductor `conductor guide --text`.
  For LoomYard: creel injects into a live pane today; this would queue guidance for the next producer's prompt instead.
- **Batched operator questions with recorded assumptions** — Conductor `questions` step and Spec Kit `/clarify`.
  Spec Kit asks at most 5 multiple-choice questions ranked by impact × uncertainty, each with a recommended answer, and logs answers in a dated Clarifications section.
  Conductor records unanswered questions as assumptions.
  For LoomYard: Discussion-Write's ask-the-operator protocol and the decision record.
- **Proactive rate-limit wait** — oh-my-claudecode (`src/features/rate-limit-wait/daemon.ts`).
  It reads the 5h/weekly usage windows and their reset times, then resumes blocked panes when the window resets.
  For LoomYard: tender schedules the resume instead of waiting for `revive`.
- **Standing goals and scheduled routines** — ORCH goals (`src/domain/goal.ts`, `seedAutonomousTasks`), [CAO](https://github.com/awslabs/cli-agent-orchestrator) cron flows with a gate script (`docs/flows.md`), and Fusion routines (README only).
  For LoomYard: board plus orch, for periodic triage, dependency bumps or `selfreport` sweeps.

## Worktree lifecycle hooks and safety (fabric, batten, Merge-In)

- **User lifecycle hooks** — [dmux](https://github.com/standardagents/dmux) (`src/utils/hooks.ts`, `context/HOOKS.md`).
  Executable hooks named `worktree_created`, `before_worktree_remove`, `pre_merge`, `post_merge`, `run_test` and others are looked up in a team dir (`.dmux-hooks/`), then a local dir, then a global one.
  They receive the slug, worktree path, branch and target branch as env vars.
  For LoomYard: `fabric add` and batten could run hub-configured hooks after pair creation (copy `.env`, install dependencies) and around Merge-In/landing.
  Today fabric installs only its own post-checkout drift hook.
- **Commit-time reservation guard** — [ntm](https://github.com/Dicklesworthstone/ntm) (`ntm guards check --staged`).
  A pre-commit hook refuses commits touching files another agent holds.
  For LoomYard: an enforcement point for the glyph leases above.
- **Sensitive-path deny-list before commit** — ccswarm (README "Safety").
  It blocks `.env`, `*.pem`, `id_rsa`, `credentials*` and `secrets.y*ml`.
  For LoomYard: a cheap check in `record-batch` and the fabric commit path.
- **Free a paused task's worktree** — [claude-squad](https://github.com/smtg-ai/claude-squad) (`session/instance.go`).
  Pause commits a dirty tree, removes the worktree and keeps the branch; resume recreates it.
  For LoomYard: tender/hibernate for long-parked runs; the weft sibling makes this harder.

## Agent sessions (reed, shuttle)

- **Status from hooks rather than pane scraping** — [agent-of-empires](https://github.com/agent-of-empires/agent-of-empires) (`src/hooks/status_file.rs`).
  Claude hooks write `running`/`waiting`/`idle` to per-instance sidecar files, and pane reconciliation fills the gaps.
  For LoomYard: shuttle already reads the Stop payload; adding a "waiting for input" sidecar could replace screen heuristics.
- **Reference status patterns and a paste pitfall** — CAO (`providers/claude_code.py`, `docs/inbox-delivery.md`).
  Regexes cover the spinner, the idle prompt, `↑/↓ to navigate` (an open question), plan approval, the trust and bypass dialogs, and "Newer model available".
  Bracketed paste behaves differently in tmux below and above 3.7.
  For LoomYard: compare against shuttle's startup-gate and readiness handling and creel inject.
- **Context forecasting and rotation for every session** — ntm (`docs/context-forecast.md`, `docs/compaction-recovery.md`).
  It warns at over 70% occupancy with under 15 minutes projected, and re-injects a refresher after "Conversation compacted".
  For LoomYard: the orch watcher's cycle, extended to the long-lived webster Master and the loom driver.
- **Edit-loop detector** — Bernstein (`docs/operations/agent-loop-detection.md`).
  It kills an agent that edits the same file 4 or more times within 5 minutes.
  For LoomYard: reed's watchdog or shuttle.
- **Destructive-command policy as a PreToolUse hook** — ntm (README §5).
  It is injected via `--settings` on every launch and holds even in bypass mode.
  For LoomYard: shuttle launch settings, if the agents' deny lists do not already cover this.
- **Staggered spawns** — ntm spaces launches by learned rate limits (README only, algorithm not read).
  For LoomYard: webster fork pacing and batten fan-out.

## Observability and audit (report, weft)

- **Hash-chained, replay-verifiable run journal** — Bernstein (`docs/operations/deterministic-replay.md`).
  `bernstein replay latest --verify` names the first step that diverges, and an Ed25519 run receipt verifies offline.
  For LoomYard: a hash chain over producer outputs in weft would make an archived `archive/<slug>/<tip>` tag self-verifying.
- **Unverified-completion rate** — Bernstein (`docs/operations/verification-tracking.md`).
  It alerts when more than 30% of completions in a window had no test, gate or signal check.
  For LoomYard: a new `lyx report` view.
- **Commit-to-record links via git notes** — [AgentNote](https://github.com/wasabeef/AgentNote).
  It attaches the session record behind each commit as a git note on a dedicated ref, plus a commit trailer.
  For LoomYard: a trailer or note on each warp batch commit pointing at its weft record path, so `git log` on the code leads to the run.
- **Run diff** — ccswarm `run diff <a> <b>`.
  For LoomYard: `lyx report` comparing two archived runs' timelines and token use.
- **OpenTelemetry tracing** — Conductor.
  For LoomYard: optional spans per producer, alongside `report timing`.

## UI and notifications (orch, tender, board)

- **Web dashboard and push notifications** — agent-of-empires (`docs/guides/web-dashboard.md`, `docs/push-notifications.md`) and ralphex `--serve` (SSE live output, late-join history).
  agent-of-empires adds tunnel access with a rotating token, a phone QR pairing code, a read-only mode, and Web Push on waiting/error with a cooldown.
  For LoomYard: a read-only view over board, `shed status` and creel, and a push when a run reaches PR-Gate, circling or a halt.
  [ralphex notifications](https://github.com/umputun/ralphex) (Slack, Telegram, webhook, custom script) are a lighter first step.
- **Attention feed with acknowledgement states** — ntm (`docs/attention-feed-contract.md`).
  It is a durable stream of items needing the human, each NEW/SEEN/SNOOZED/ACK/DISMISSED, with cursors.
  For LoomYard: a single "what is waiting on me" list across runs for the operator and the orch.
- **Terminal bell on a waiting gate** — Conductor's fleet TUI.
  For LoomYard: a near-free signal from reed when PR-Gate or a parent review is waiting.

## Spec and discussion review (Discussion-Write, Discussion review, stencils)

- **Requirements-quality checklist** — Spec Kit `/checklist` ("unit tests for English").
  Items tagged Completeness/Clarity/Consistency/Measurability/Gap/Traceability carry IDs, cite requirements, and are answered by the reviewer, never ticked by the writer.
  For LoomYard: an artifact the Discussion-review judge must answer item by item.
- **Fixed analysis categories** — [Kiro Analyze Requirements](https://kiro.dev/docs/specs/analyze-requirements/).
  It checks for inconsistency, ambiguity, functional/non-functional conflicts, unstated assumptions and missing edge cases.
  For LoomYard: name these lenses in the Discussion-review stencil.
- **Versioned constitution fed to reviewers** — Spec Kit `constitution`.
  It carries a semver version, amendment dates and a sync-impact report, and its MUST rules feed every analysis.
  For LoomYard: PATTERN.md is enforced by Go tests; handing its rules to plan and code reviewers as numbered MUSTs is the new part.
- **Glob-scoped steering context** — [Kiro steering](https://kiro.dev/docs/steering/).
  Context files load always, on a `fileMatch` glob, manually, or by description match, and support `#[[file:path:12-28]]` includes.
  For LoomYard: stencils could pull in per-area guidance chosen by the paths of a plan's glyphs.
- **Living spec and critique before execution** — [Augment Intent](https://www.augmentcode.com/intent).
  A Critique specialist reviews the spec for feasibility before implementers start, and the spec updates as work lands.
  LoomYard's Discussion and Plan reviews already cover the critique.
  Intent is closed source and Augment says Critique's checks are "not yet fully documented", so nothing more is verifiable.

entries.title: Git test fixtures trip Cortex XDR on the work laptop
entries.brief: Parallel git-heavy tests create so many files at once that Cortex XDR killed VS Code and then crashed itself, twice; tests must stay usable on a machine with endpoint protection
entries.body:
## Seen (operator report, 2026-10-16)

On the operator work laptop, which runs Cortex XDR, the git tests create so many files at once that XDR flagged them as malware behaviour.
Twice it terminated all of VS Code, and both times XDR itself crashed afterwards, so the machine had to be restarted.

For scale, on the home machine a parallel `lyx gate test --tags integration ./...` (gate `go_parallel: 4`) takes 56s, and the serial package-by-package total is 156s (`docs/benchmarks/test-suite-weight.md`, which also counts git fixture and code subprocesses per package).

## Idea (orch recommendation, not a decision)

- Short term: on that machine set the machine-local gate layer, `lyx config gate --layer local --set go_parallel=1` and `--set slots=1`, so one package and one test run go at a time.
- Check on the laptop whether that is enough, since XDR may react to the file-creation rate within one package as well.
- If not: make the git fixtures create fewer files (shared fixtures built once per package, cloned or copied less), and measure files created per package so the heaviest are known.

entries.title: Rename the lyx binary to lyr (name clash with LyX)
entries.body:
Imported from [issue #670](https://github.com/Knatte18/loomyard/issues/670).

`lyx` collides with LyX, the LaTeX editor, which ships as the `lyx` package in Ubuntu/Debian and installs `/usr/bin/lyx`.
On a machine with both, whichever comes first on PATH wins: a shell where `~/go/bin` is not yet on PATH starts the LaTeX editor instead of LoomYard.
LyX is common among researchers, so the clash is likely for other users too.

Operator decision 2026-10-17: rename the binary to `lyr` (LoomYard Runner), replacing the first proposal `lyd`.
Checked 2026-10-17: `lyr` is no Ubuntu package name, is not installed on the operator's machine, and a web search found no CLI tool whose binary is named `lyr`.
Rejected: `warp` and `ply` are Ubuntu packages, `weft` and `warp` are already fabric terms here, and the four-letter weaving names (`pirn`, `sley`) are longer to type.

Scope: the `cmd/lyx` build target and `binaryName()` in `tools/deploy`, docs and README, stencils and skills in the `ly` plugin that invoke `lyx`, and any scripts or launchers that call it.

entries.title: Language-neutral gate: lyx gate run takes a slot for any command
entries.brief: The gate slot pool covers only go test; a C# or Python hub verify bypasses it. Add lyx gate run -- cmd and per-language parallelism.
entries.body:
## Seen (orch, 2026-10-17)

`lyx gate test` runs only `go test`: it takes a hub gate slot, then runs `go test -p <go_parallel>` over the named packages.
A hub in another language has no gate, so its verify command (for example `dotnet test` in a C# hub) runs outside the slot pool.
Several runs then build and test at once with no limit, which is what the slot pool exists to stop.

## Idea

- `lyx gate run -- <cmd>`: take a gate slot, run any command, release the slot.
  The language-specific verbs (`lyx gate test` for Go) become thin wrappers over it.
- Parallelism per language in `language.yaml`, in place of the Go-only `go_parallel`.
- Each language's verify commands and test tiers are declared by the hub, never hard-coded in lyx.

## Operator view, not a decision (2026-10-17)

- lyx is to support Python as well: Go, C# and Python are the three languages in the first round.
- Layered test tiers matter in C# too; see note `dotnet-scoped-verify` for the tiers in the operator's work repository.

- Scoped tests are extremely important: a C# hub cannot run its full suite.

## Orch recommendation, not a decision (2026-10-17)

The slot pool in `internal/gateslot` is already language-neutral (one file lock per slot); only `lyx gate test` on top of it is Go-specific.

1. `lyx gate run -- <cmd>`: take a slot, run any command, release; a nested run inherits the parent slot through the existing environment variable. `lyx gate test` becomes the Go form of it.
2. The hub declares its test tiers in `language.yaml`: name, command and when each runs (card, final, Publish, baseline), with placeholders such as `{parallel}` and `{targets}`, so lyx knows no tool. Examples: `dotnet test --filter {targets} -maxcpucount:{parallel}`, `pytest -n {parallel} {targets}`, `go test -p {parallel} {targets}`. `go_parallel` becomes a general `parallel`.
3. Test selection per language behind one interface: Go has `internal/impactset`; C# needs what note `dotnet-scoped-verify` describes; Python could use `pytest-testmon` or the import graph.
4. The shell guard refuses raw `dotnet test` and `pytest` as it refuses raw module-wide `go test`, so every run goes through the gate.
5. The regression tier (note `regression-baseline-verify`) uses the same tier mechanism.

Order: 1, 2, 4 first; 3 and 5 are the large ones and come separately.

## Related

Notes `dotnet-verify-protocol` and `dotnet-scoped-verify`.

entries.title: Regression tier: baseline profiles before the run, compare at the final gate
entries.brief: Support a hub regression tier that writes profiles on the parent before implementation and compares after, switchable per task for expected drift.
entries.body:
## Seen (operator, 2026-10-17)

The operator's C# work repository has a regression tier: a suite run before the implementation writes profiles, and the same suite run after it compares against them to catch drift.
Many tasks there are pure refactorings that must not change behaviour, and this tier is what proves it.
Operator view, not a decision: regression tests are not always wanted, since some tasks expect drift, for example when a model is changed; this must be handled, perhaps by a flag on the task in the board.

## Orch recommendation, not a decision

- A per-task setting in the board entry's `run_settings`, with three values:
  - `off`: no baseline, no compare.
  - `preserve`: any drift fails the final gate, as a verify failure.
  - `expect-drift`: baseline and compare still run, but the drift report goes to the reviewers and the alignment agent, who judge whether it matches the task's goal; drift alone fails nothing.
  The hub's default lives in config.
- The hub declares the tier in `language.yaml` as three commands: the profile generator, the compare (the repository's own tool, with its tolerances) and the profile directory. lyx only orchestrates and knows no format.
- Operator view, not a decision: the baseline belongs in shed as a producer; it often takes long, so it should start at the beginning as an async command while Discussion and the rest run.
- Orch recommendation, not a decision: shed runs one producer at a time today, so async becomes a generic shed pair of ordinary producers, usable by any recipe:
  - `Job-Start` (a side action with a config flag) starts a detached job, records its handle in run state and returns at once.
  - `Job-Join` waits for the job and fails with its log when it failed.
- Operator view, not a decision: the baseline runs in the task worktree itself, since loom changes no code before Webster, and its output goes to a gitignored place such as `.scratch/`; large simulation time series are never committed.
- Operator decision 2026-10-17: `Job-Join` sits right before Webster, the first row that changes code, so Webster never edits or builds (`bin/`, `obj/`) while the baseline still runs; when Discussion and Plan take longer than the baseline, the join costs nothing.
- Operator view, not a decision: fixed rows in loom for a case that may never come feel clumsy, but each only checks its flag and moves on in milliseconds when it is off.
- Precedent: batten's Open-Window, Seed-IDE and Open-IDE are such rows today, `shedadapters`' switched producer behind a `batten.yaml` flag read from the pair's config stack, so a task's `run_settings` sets it per task. Unlike those, `Job-Join` must be able to fail the run, since the switched producer only warns.
- The job takes a gate slot like every test run, and obeys a hub pause like the run's other work (note `pause-background-work`).
- Batten tears the job down with the run.
- The compare runs at the final gate only, never per card, to keep the cost down.

## Stations (operator view, not a decision, 2026-10-17)

Loom's recipe could hold fixed command boxes of one type, each taking several entries set per repository:

- Before Discussion: a box that starts the async regression suite, which writes the baseline. The IDE and terminal rows may be their own box of the same type; they stay in any case.
- Right before Webster: a box that only waits for the regression suite to finish.
- Before Finalize: a box that checks whether the regression passed. What it does when it did not is the open hard part.

## On a failed compare (orch recommendation, not a decision)

- Place the compare right after the Webster review (before Describe and Merge-In), not before Finalize: the baseline and the code then share one parent, so drift from other tasks landed meanwhile never enters the compare, which settles the parent-move question.
- Operator view, not a decision: a jump back to `Webster-Burler-Review` on a failed compare is jumping around, and not clean.
- `preserve`: the compare is its own perch, built like every other perch: a check row that runs the compare command, and a fix row that gets the drift report as its finding and hands back to the check. It loops under its own caps and escalates to the orch past them, with no jump into another segment.
- Operator view, not a decision (stated as very important): when regression is not needed, all of it is skipped completely.
  Orch recommendation, not a decision: with `off`, or no regression tier in the hub's `language.yaml`, every regression row is a no-show that reads its setting and is Done: no job starts, no slot is taken, no build runs and no agent is spawned; a hub with no regression tier never shows these rows in its status.
- Operator view, not a decision: a perch in loom's main line starts whatever happens, so it is not skipped by itself.
  Orch recommendation, not a decision: skip it the way darn skips its review perch today: with `review_max_bounces` 0, `internal/loomrecipe` rewrites Darn-Write's Done edge straight to Merge-In when the recipe loads (see `contracts/recipes/darn-recipe.yaml`), so the perch rows are never entered. With regression off for the task or the hub, the edge into the regression perch is rewritten past it the same way, and the task's `run_settings` sets it per task.
  The perch's check row runs the compare command, not an LLM judge, so even when it is entered no agent starts until the compare fails.
- Operator view, not a decision: a compare that finds no drift is skipped onward too.
  Orch recommendation, not a decision: under `preserve` the check row passes and the fix row never runs, so no agent is spawned. Under `expect-drift`, no drift is itself worth a line to PR-Align, since a model change that moves no numbers may not have taken effect.
- `expect-drift`: the compare fails nothing; the drift report goes to PR-Align, where the alignment agent judges it against the task's goal and escalates when it cannot tell.

## Open

- How long the generator takes on the work machine, and whether it can be scoped like the other tiers.
- Whether `preserve` should also run the compare per batch, to point at the card that caused drift.
- A parent that moves during the run is merged in at Merge-In, after the baseline was taken: drift from other landed tasks then shows in the compare. Re-take the baseline at the new parent, or accept it as a known limit.

## Related

Notes `gate-language-neutral` and `dotnet-scoped-verify`.

entries.title: Key-rename migration never reaches the hub config: loom-model-key-names silently turned off the hub fans
entries.body:
Imported from [issue #709](https://github.com/Knatte18/loomyard/issues/709).

## Seen

After `loom-model-key-names` landed (`a273d69bc`), the hub's `_board/_lyx/config/loom.yaml` and `darn.yaml` still held the old key names (`review`, `discussion_review`, `webster_fan`, `merge_fix_fan`, darn `review_fan`, ...).
The new keys resolved from the template, so every run silently lost the hub's lens fan, twill fixer and reviewer models: `lyx config loom --resolved` showed `webster_reviewer_fan: "" # template` and the old keys as `# default`.

- `lyx config reconcile` in the prime reports loom with no `migrated` entry: it never reaches the hub default layer.
- `lyx config reconcile` (dry-run) run from `_board/` does list the loom renames, but treats the hub files as a worktree layer: it would strip most keys and mark `darn`, `gate`, `landing`, `language`, `fabric` and `board` as retired, so `--apply` there is unsafe.
- Nothing at landing or deploy ran the migration, and nothing warned that the hub file held unknown keys.

## Workaround

The orch carried every value to its new name by hand with `lyx config loom --layer default --set ...` and `lyx config darn --layer default --set ...`.
The old keys stay in both files as `preserved` entries, since `--set` cannot remove a key.

## Expected

A key-rename migration reaches the hub's default layer, through a hub-scoped `lyx config reconcile` or at landing, and removes the old keys.
A hub config file holding keys the template no longer knows is reported loudly at load.

entries.title: One generic Command producer for every flag-gated side-action row
entries.brief: Replace OpenWindow, SeedIDE, OpenIDE and the planned Job-Start/Job-Join with one shed engine that runs a CLI command named in config, sync or async, warn or halt.
entries.body:
## Seen (orch, 2026-10-17)

Batten's Open-Window, Seed-IDE and Open-IDE rows share one Go type, `SwitchedProducer` in `internal/shedadapters`, but each is its own registry engine (`OpenWindow`, `SeedIDE`, `OpenIDE`) wrapping a told Go action behind a told `batten.yaml` flag.
A new side action therefore needs a new engine, a new Go action and a new flag.
Other places already run a shell command from config inside a bigger row: `landing.yaml`'s `deploy` (Land) and `publish_verify` (Publish), and darn's `verify`.
Note `regression-baseline-verify` adds `Job-Start` and `Job-Join`, which would be two more such rows.

## Operator view, not a decision (2026-10-17)

All these special rows should be one and the same producer whose only job is to run a CLI command; the flag and the command to run can live somewhere else entirely, in config.

## Orch recommendation, not a decision

- One registry engine, `Command`, used by every such row. The row names a config key; the key holds the command, with placeholders such as `{slug}` and `{pair}`. An empty command is the off switch, so no separate flag is needed.
- Per row, in the recipe: the failure policy (`warn`, as the IDE rows do today, or `halt`) and the mode (`sync`, or `async`, which starts the command detached and records its handle).
- A `Join` form of the same engine waits for an `async` row's handle and applies its failure policy; this is `Job-Join`.
- Each action that is Go code today gets a `lyx` verb (for example the terminal window and the IDE seed), so the default config spells it as a command.
- Later candidates: `deploy` and `publish_verify` as their own `Command` rows instead of commands buried in Land and Publish.

## Open

- Whether a task's `run_settings` may set the command, or only switch it on and off; a command from a board entry runs on the machine, so it may need the same trust class as `deploy`.
- Placeholders: which run facts a command may name.

## Related

Notes `regression-baseline-verify`, `gate-language-neutral`.

entries.title: Entry gate on shed rows: a check decides whether a row runs at all
entries.brief: Replace darn recipe edge rewrite and the switched producer flag check with one shed entry gate per row; false means Done without acting.
entries.body:
## Seen (orch, 2026-10-17)

Two ways exist today to leave out a row that is not wanted:

- Darn turns its review perch off by a recipe rewrite: with `review_max_bounces` 0, `internal/loomrecipe` rewrites Darn-Write's Done edge straight to Merge-In when the recipe loads (`contracts/recipes/darn-recipe.yaml`), so the perch rows are never entered.
- Batten's Open-Window, Seed-IDE and Open-IDE rows are `shedadapters`' switched producer: the row reads its `batten.yaml` flag and is Done without acting when the flag is off.

## Operator view, not a decision (2026-10-17)

The recipe rewrite is a terrible solution.
A Bouncer should instead have an entry gate: a check that runs first and decides whether the Bouncer runs at all.
For darn's perch that check is only whether `review_max_bounces` is above 0, and the producer that opens VS Code works the same way: it checks its flag and skips everything when the flag is off.

## Orch recommendation, not a decision

- The entry gate belongs in shed, for every row, since every FSM needs it: a row in the recipe may name an entry check, read from the run's config stack when the row is reached; when it is false, the row is Done without acting and the run follows its Done edge.
  A perch's Burler row is reached only through the Bouncer's stuck edge, so a skipped Bouncer skips the whole perch.
- Status and the run's history record the row as skipped with the check's reason, so a skip is visible.
- The switched producer's flag check becomes this gate, and `internal/loomrecipe`'s edge rewrite for darn is removed.
- The regression perch (note `regression-baseline-verify`) and the `Command` rows (note `command-producer`) use the same gate.

## Where it sits (2026-10-17)

Operator view, not a decision: the recipe rewrite is not clean at all; every producer should be able to carry an entry gate, set in the one template all producers share.

Orch recommendation, not a decision, from the code:

- Every row is already one shared shape: `shedbuild.Row` in the recipe (`internal/shedbuild/recipe.go`) and `shedengine.ProducerDef` in the engine (`internal/shedengine/producer.go`), which carry each row's routing (`OnDone`, `OnStuck`, `OnReroute`) and budget around the `ShedProducer` seam.
- The entry gate goes there, as one more field beside the routing: an `entry_gate` key on `Row` and its counterpart on `ProducerDef`.
- Shed's loop checks the gate before it calls `ShedProducer.Call`; a false gate records the row as skipped and follows `OnDone`, so no producer implements anything, and every row of every recipe gets the gate for free.
- The `ShedProducer` interface itself stays one method, `Call`.

## The check's form (orch recommendation, not a decision)

- Reading config: shed knows no config, so the gate reads through the one told lookup task `shedrecipe-capabilities` adds, `Setting(module, key)`, filled by the recipe's owner from the pair's config stack, a task's `run_settings` included. The gate is read when the row is reached, never when the recipe loads, so a setting changed mid-run counts.
- A small fixed form, no expression language:
  - `darn.review_max_bounces`: true when the value is set and not zero, false, empty or an empty list.
  - `regression.mode != off` and `== <value>`: one comparison against a literal.
  - A list of such checks: all must hold.
  - No or, no arithmetic, no free code: a case that needs more gets a setting of its own.
- Recipe load refuses a gate naming an unknown module or key, as `shedrecipe-capabilities` refuses unknown keys.
- Examples: Darn-Review `entry_gate: darn.review_max_bounces`; Open-IDE `entry_gate: batten.open_ide`; a regression row `entry_gate: [loom.regression_mode != off]`.

## Open

- The form of a check: a config key that must be true or above 0, or a small fixed set of predicates; never free code.
- Whether a task's `run_settings` can switch a gate per task: it can today for darn's budget and batten's flags, since both read the pair's config stack.

entries.title: Preflight pushes the weft branch synchronously and races the board sync
entries.brief: Preflight spent 11 s mostly in a weft push to GitHub, refused once after 8 s; push detached or serialise with the board sync.
entries.body:
## Seen (orch, 2026-10-17)

The darn run `creel-c13-stacked-rewrite` spent 11.1 s in its Preflight row (trace `acc61c4a8e5651cb` in the pair's `.lyx/logs/`), almost all of it in a synchronous push of the weft branch to GitHub:

- 13:43:50.98: the row commits the weft (`fabric: mutation kind=commit_created`); 0.2 s earlier the same step spawned a detached board sync, which pushes to the same records repository.
- 13:43:58.91: the first push of `creel-c13-stacked-rewrite-weft` is refused after 8 s: `! [remote rejected] ... (failed)`.
- 13:44:01.89: the retry succeeds after 3 s, and the row is Done.

The operator saw about 22 s for the row; the trace accounts for 11 s of it.

## Idea

- Nothing in the run reads the remote weft branch until Publish, so Preflight could push it detached, as the board sync already is, and leave the row at local work only.
- The 8 s refusal looks like two pushes to the same records repository at once (the board sync and the weft push); if so, serialising them, or the detached push, would remove the retry.

## A pair begun on another machine

Operator question 2026-10-17: what if the branches already exist because the task was begun on another machine?
That case is settled before Preflight, at `fabricengine.Add` (Worktree-Create), per `internal/fabricengine/doc.go`: it probes both origins read-only, adopts a live pair (fast-forwards a local weft branch behind origin, or makes origin's weft and warp branches local tracking branches), refuses a true divergence with `ErrRemoteLeftover`, and never force-pushes or deletes a live pair's branches.
`Add` itself already pushes nothing and leaves the push to the pair's detached push (`SpawnPairPush`).
So a detached Preflight push changes nothing for that case; it only gives up seeing at once a push the remote refuses, which the next detached push logs as a Warn.
The bare `(failed)` refusal is a known server-side race: every plain fabric push retries it with backoff.

## Open

- Whether the remote refusal is a GitHub race between the two pushes or something else; check other runs' Preflight traces for the same warning.

entries.title: A darn writer cannot rerun a verify tier it is refused, so a flaky tier failure loops and escalates
entries.body:
Imported from [issue #714](https://github.com/Knatte18/loomyard/issues/714).

## What happened

`lyx loom` halted `blocked` (anomaly `escalation-to-human`) at Publish.
`publish_verify` failed after merging the parent branch with `internal/reedengine` `TestBoot_TmuxConf/AppendingFileIsSourcedOncePerServerStart/TwoWorktreesBootedConcurrently` reporting `run list-commands: exit status 1: server exited unexpectedly`.
The task's diff did not touch `internal/reedengine`, so the failure looks like a race in booting two tmux servers concurrently, not a defect of the change.

## Why it is abnormal

- The test is flaky and fails an unrelated task at the Publish gate.
- The Darn-Write agent could not reproduce or fix it: the test carries the `tmux` build tag, and tmux-tier go runs are refused in a darn session.
  The agent handed off with no commit, so the run escalated to a human with a failure the darn step can never resolve.

## What to do

- Make `TwoWorktreesBootedConcurrently` deterministic, or retry or isolate the tmux server start it races on.
- Consider whether a darn session facing a verify failure only in a tier it cannot run should get a way to rerun it, or should be told up front to escalate, rather than looping through the Darn cycle first.

Provenance: task `stencilstore-dev-warning-noise`; notes `Darn-Write.md`, `loom-halt.md`.

entries.title: shedverbs wait-world integration tests flake: loop exited before it recorded itself
entries.body:
Imported from [issue #716](https://github.com/Knatte18/loomyard/issues/716).

Two consecutive Merge-In verifies failed in the `internal/shedverbs` integration tier, on different wait-world tests.
Each failure had the waiter reporting `loop … exited before it recorded itself`.
The loom run halted blocked at Merge-In (`escalation-to-human`) with the way forward `lyx loom goto --to Darn-Write`, then `lyx loom resume`.

Why it is abnormal: the failures did not reproduce in isolation, under `-race`, under `-count=300` or beside heavy integration packages, so diagnosing them cost several runs.
The likely cause is the wait-world fixture's 20 ms `LockGrace`, which the waiter's free-lock probe can exhaust under scheduling stalls.

What to do: give the wait-world fixture the production lock grace (the task's fix did this), and check other fixtures in the integration tier for short grace values that make verify nondeterministic.

Provenance: task `gate-wait-cache-cap`, notes `Darn-Write.md`, `loom-halt.md`.

entries.title: Recurring Webster kick-start pack (glyph) audit
entries.brief: Re-run tools/forkaudit on new Webster forks to track pack use and correctness
entries.body:
## What this is

A recurring audit of how Webster implementer forks use their kick-start pack (glyph spans) and whether the pack is correct, run with `tools/forkaudit/forkaudit.sh --since <date> --pack-check --plan`.
Each audit keeps its report and summary under `docs/research/glyph-audit-<date>/`.
Operator instruction 2026-10-17: keep this on the board so future glyph audits are not forgotten.

## Audits so far

- `docs/research/glyph-audit-2026-10-12/`, `-10-13/`, `-10-15/`: the inline, read-all-first and pack-file layouts.
- `docs/research/glyph-audit-2026-10-17/`: the first audit of the per-card layout (`lyx loom card-pack`, default since `aa925bdcc`), 90 forks from 26 runs.
  Card forks read about half their spans before the first edit (pack-file forks a quarter) and start editing after half as many calls; 0 stale spans of 1661 checked at batch start; about 20% of edits still go to files with no span; cost per card is higher, but the workloads differ.

## Open points for the next audit

- `forkaudit` grades only a fork's first `card-pack` call, so files a later card's pack covered count as missed, and the 20% missed share is an upper bound (open finding from `aa925bdcc`, in `tools/forkaudit/pack-entries.jq` and `report.jq`).
- The card arm's spans-window definition may bias the spans-reached share (open finding from `aa925bdcc`, in `tools/forkaudit/extract.jq`).
- Pack drift during a batch is unmeasured.
- Five forks in the 2026-10-17 sample matched no arm marker (`none`).
- Three card forks had no spans at all, among them a creel-core fork with 81 edits; why is unknown.

## Orch recommendation, not a decision

Run the next audit after about 20 more Webster runs, or right after any change to the pack layout or the fork prompt, whichever comes first, and fix the first-call grading gap in `forkaudit` before it, so the missed-files share means something.
A cheap model (Sonnet) runs the script; the orch places the result in `docs/research/`.

entries.title: Remove the Webster kick-start pack
entries.brief: Drop every kick-start pack layout and its code; glyphs stay in the plan and its gates
entries.body:
## Operator decision 2026-10-17

Remove the Webster kick-start pack, every layout of it (inline, pack file, per card), with its code and config keys.
Glyphs stay in the plan and in the plan gates.
Until the code is removed, the hub's `webster.yaml` sets `kickstart_pack: false` (operator, 2026-10-17, `_board` commit `2d850b341`).
Quarry stays its own repository for now, since it changes rarely (operator, 2026-10-17).

## Evidence

- Four audits, `docs/research/glyph-audit-2026-10-12/`, `-10-13/`, `-10-15/`, `-10-17/`: no layout lowered exploration against no pack (exploration calls per card 5.2 without a pack, 5.8 to 7 with one; calls before the first edit 7 against 4 to 8.5), and the per-card layout costs more per card than the older ones on a different workload.
- A sample of 9 per-card forks (2026-10-17): the forks work file by file and read a file just before editing it; of the spans not read before the first edit, 59% were read later, 23% never read while the file was edited from the fork's own grep, `sed` or build errors, 18% not needed or already covered.
  Several forks grepped for sites the pack had already listed, and none mentioned the pack.
- Webster is about a third of a loom run's active time (`lyx report timing` since 2026-10-10, 105 landed runs: median 30% per run), and reading code is a small part of it.

## Orch recommendation, not a decision

- Keep `tools/forkaudit` working for runs without a pack, so a no-pack baseline can be measured.
- Forks never call `lyx quarry` in any audit since the pack; resolve's value is in the plan gates, which call quarry in code.
- Note `enclose-checks` (formerly `enclose-kickstart`) lost its pack use with this removal and now proposes Enclose for mechanical checks instead.

entries.title: Use quarry Enclose for mechanical checks: verify failures to plan cards
entries.brief: Map tool-output file:line to member glyphs, then to the card and batch that changed them
entries.body:
Operator, 2026-10-08: quarry gains `Enclose`, written as quarry's task `enclose-locations` (in the quarry repo; the operator spawns it).
It maps `file:line` ranges from tool output to the innermost enclosing member glyphs, with the same Symbol data `Resolve` returns, also at a git revision (`quarry enclose [--rev R]`).
Markdown is out of its scope: a `.md` location is a per-item rejection.

## Change of direction, 2026-10-17

The original use was a kick-start pack of the failing members for recovery agents and fixers.
The pack measurement this waited on (operator decisions 2026-10-11 and 2026-10-15) came in with `docs/research/glyph-audit-2026-10-17/`: forks read code themselves whatever the pack holds, and note `kickstart-pack-remove` records the operator decision to remove the pack.
A pack of failing members is dropped with it: a fork given `file:line` reads around it in one call.

Operator view, not a decision: Enclose can be useful for mechanical checks, where Loomyard's own code needs to know which member a line belongs to, with no agent in the loop.

## Orch recommendation, not a decision

First use, which changes no flow: a verify failure at Merge-In or Publish is mapped through Enclose to its member glyph, then to the plan card whose targets hold that glyph and the batch and commit that ran the card (`_lyx/webster/state.json`).
The fixer's brief names that card, its intent and its commit, as a starting point instead of the whole diff.
Later possibilities, each its own decision:

- Re-run only the batch that made the failing change (`lyx webster reset --batch` and a fresh fork with the failure attached), instead of a whole-diff review round.
- A finding that cites `path:line` is mapped to a glyph at the reviewed revision, so later edits never shift it, and it can be checked against the plan's targets.
- A failure in a member no card targets is reported as a scope gap: the plan missed it.
- Test, vet and lint failures are grouped per member, so duplicate findings fold.

Measure that a fixer uses the named card before building more, as the pack showed agents may read and ignore such hints.

Glyph↔path conversion stays in quarry; Loomyard never intersects lines with symbol spans itself.

## Quarry's Enclose as delivered (quarry PR #36, 2026-10-08)

- Released in quarry v0.3.0: `(*Repo).Enclose(locs)` and `(*Repo).EncloseAt(rev, locs)`, with `EncloseResult`, `EncloseReasons` and `RenderEncloseJSON`; paths are relative to the repo root, not the cwd, and an unknown rev fails the whole call.
- They take location spellings (`path:N`, `path:N-M`, `path:N:col`), not structs; Loomyard formats tool-output locations into them.
- Rejections carry a closed reason set (`EncloseReasons`), including `unaddressable` for a `.go` file in the repo root or a path containing `#`; Loomyard cites `path:line` for any rejected item.
- A `found` glyph may not Resolve afterwards (an explicitly named gitignored file, a file without a package clause, a path through a symlinked directory; `quarry/enclose.go`). Loomyard treats a Resolve miss after Enclose as "no current span", never as an error, the same as a member the fixer deleted or renamed.
- Loomyard pins quarry v0.2.1; this task bumps `go.mod` to v0.3.0, which has no other breaking change.

entries.title: lyx board rename: change an entry slug in one write
entries.brief: Rename an entry keeping all fields and rewriting depends_on; report prose mentions
entries.body:
## Seen

`lyx board` has no verb that changes an entry's slug.
Renaming `enclose-kickstart` to `enclose-checks` (2026-10-17) took `get --body` to a file, a `merge` with `remove_slugs` and an upsert carrying the old entry's title, brief, kind, labels and `created`, then a manual fix of the old slug in another entry's body.

## Idea

A verb `lyx board rename {slug, to}` that renames an entry in one atomic write, keeping its body, kind, labels, priority, issues, `created` and every other field, and rewrites the old slug in every other task's `depends_on`.
It refuses a run-held entry, as the run lock does for any scope change, and a target slug that exists or breaks the slug length limit.
It reports the entries whose body or brief still mention the old slug, since prose references are not rewritten.

entries.title: lyx report timing leaves out darn runs
entries.brief: Report darn runs beside loom runs, with phases from the recipe
entries.body:
## Seen (orch, 2026-10-17)

`lyx report timing --since 2026-10-01` lists 161 runs and none of the darn runs that landed in that window: `gate-wait-cache-cap`, `landing-trailer-text` and `stencilstore-dev-warning-noise`, among others, are absent from `.runs`.
Its phase columns are loom's (setup, discussion, plan, webster, merge, publish-finalize, land), so a darn run's rows (Darn-Write, Darn-Bouncer, Darn-Burler-Review, Darn-Burler-Fix) have no column either.
To compare darn with loom, the orch read each darn run's last batten `status.json` from the records repository's history instead: 29 darn runs, median span from first to last history entry 22 minutes (15 to 31), sleep and waits not taken out, against a loom active-time median of 108 minutes.

## Idea

- `lyx report timing` reports darn runs beside loom runs, tagged with their recipe, with the same sleep and wait accounting.
- Darn's rows map to phases of their own (such as write and review), or the report's phase set comes from the recipe, so a new recipe needs no report change.
- `lyx report convergence` is checked for the same gap.

entries.title: Remove the per-package test budget; watch suite growth by a recurring test-time audit
entries.brief: test-budget.yaml forces no reviewed decision and serializes plans; remove it
entries.body:
## Seen (2026-10-17)

- `test-tiers` (D9, 2026-10-07) added a per-package test-count budget: `cmd/lyx/testdata/test-budget.yaml`, guarded by `cmd/lyx/testbudget_test.go`, so that "guards keep the suite from regrowing unseen".
  Its bound: "a budget raise is a one-line edit in the same commit as the tests that need it, so the guard forces a visible, reviewed decision".
- No one judges a raise:
  - the alignment stencil treats the file as bookkeeping that never escalates (`contracts/stencils/loom/loom-template-alignment.md`);
  - the code reviewers are not asked to judge raises;
  - the plan review's test-economy lens (`internal/burlerengine/template.yaml`) only checks that a new test is budgeted;
  - the guard's failure names the value to set the row to, so an agent raises it and moves on.
- Cost: the file changed in 114 of 302 commits on main since 2026-10-01; 11 of 34 plans had two or more cards editing it, the largest false scheduling dependency in `docs/research/parallel-batches-2026-10-17/`; every card adding tests must list it under `Edit:` (CLAUDE.md "Test budget").
- What keeps test count down in practice is `PATTERN-test-economy`, enforced in review.

## Operator decision (2026-10-17)

The budget has no purpose: remove it.

## Idea

- Remove `cmd/lyx/testbudget_test.go`, `cmd/lyx/testdata/test-budget.yaml`, the "Test budget" section of `pattern/PATTERN-test-speed.md`, the "Test budget" section of `CLAUDE.md`, and the budget mentions in the alignment stencil and the burler test-economy lens.
- Watch suite growth instead with a recurring test-time audit on the board, measured with `cmd/testtiming` against `docs/benchmarks/test-suite-timing.md`, the way `glyph-audit-recurring` tracks glyph use.

### Orch recommendation

Run it as a darn task, since it only deletes; the recurring audit is a board note, not code.
